questions.question: A team deploys a new version by deregistering the old ECS tasks from the ALB target group and stopping them immediately. Users report dropped connections and 502s during every deploy — yet health checks stay green throughout. Which mechanism did the team bypass, and what is the graceful pattern?
choices: The health-check interval (30 s) times the unhealthy threshold (2) means the ALB needs up to a minute to notice a stopped task and keeps routing to it; lowering the interval to 5 s and the threshold to 1 makes deploys near-seamless without other changes

Deregistration puts a target into a draining state: the ALB stops sending it new requests but lets in-flight ones finish, for up to deregistration_delay (default 300 s). Stopping the process immediately kills exactly those live connections — the draining window exists so old tasks can finish the work they hold. Graceful deploys stop a target only after draining completes; the lesson is that shutdown is a two-phase act — stop accepting new work, then finish the work in hand

With cross-zone load balancing enabled (the ALB default), every node routes to every target, so a deregistered task keeps receiving requests from nodes in other zones until their target lists converge; disabling cross-zone makes deregistration take effect zone-locally and instantly

Clients cache the ALB's DNS record for its 60-second TTL, so requests keep arriving at node IPs that still hold connections to the old tasks; fronting the ALB with a Route 53 alias record eliminates the client-side caching window
questions.explanation: The failure sits at the connection-lifecycle layer, not the health layer. Health checks answer 'should NEW requests go to this target?' — they say nothing about requests already in flight. Deregistration likewise governs new traffic, and provides deregistration_delay precisely so the old traffic can complete: that is connection draining, the mechanism that makes rolling deploys invisible to users. Killing the process the moment deregistration starts turns every in-flight request into a reset connection, and no health-check tuning can help because health was never the problem — the green checks throughout were the tell. Orchestrators like ECS honour the draining window automatically; deregister-then-kill by hand re-creates the failure. The distractors blame real mechanisms for the wrong failure: faster health checks only shrink detection time for targets that fail, which these didn't; cross-zone balancing changes which nodes route to which targets, but draining state applies across all nodes either way; and DNS TTL governs how clients find ALB nodes, not how the ALB manages its own server-side connections to targets.

questions.question: One EC2 host runs a web app behind NGINX on 443 — TLS, auth, and IP filtering all configured — plus Portainer bound directly to port 9443. The security group allows both 443 and 9443 from 0.0.0.0/0. A review flags Portainer as exposed; the developer objects that NGINX is the host's gatekeeper, so its protections apply. What is wrong with that mental model?
choices: NGINX only governs traffic on ports it actually serves. A request to 9443 passes the security group and lands directly on Portainer — NGINX never sees it, so none of its TLS, auth, or filtering applies. The layers are in series only along paths that traverse both: the SG decides which doors exist, and NGINX guards only the doors it stands behind. An SG-opened port with no proxy behind it is an unguarded door — restrict 9443 at the SG, or route Portainer through NGINX

The security group is misordered: the 0.0.0.0/0 rule on 9443 shadows the narrower rules. Adding an explicit deny rule for 9443 ahead of the allow restores the intended precedence, since SG rules evaluate in priority order much like NGINX location blocks

The exposure is theoretical: Portainer terminates its own TLS on 9443, so the traffic is encrypted end-to-end and at least as protected as the NGINX path; the finding is about certificate hygiene, not access control

Because security groups are stateful, connection tracking from established 443 sessions extends to 9443 flows on the same host, letting authenticated app users reach Portainer; splitting the two services onto separate ENIs with separate SGs closes the leak
questions.explanation: NGINX is a process listening on specific ports, not a host-wide filter. Defense in depth means each request passes the SG and then NGINX — but only on paths NGINX proxies. Traffic to 9443 has exactly one gate, the SG, and that gate was opened to the whole internet. The reasoning error is treating a reverse proxy as if it sat inline on the network interface like a firewall; the honest model is 'the SG decides which doors exist; NGINX guards the doors it stands behind', and the design rule follows: never leave an SG-open port pointing at an unproxied service — close it at the edge or put it behind the L7 gate. The distractors bend real mechanics: security groups are allow-only — there are no deny rules and no rule ordering, anything not explicitly allowed is implicitly denied, so 'shadowing' cannot occur; TLS provides confidentiality, not access control — an encrypted connection to an internet-reachable admin panel is still an internet-reachable admin panel; and statefulness means return traffic of an allowed connection is admitted per connection — it never links flows across different ports or grants one port's users access to another.

questions.question: During Dictionary drafting, a teammate proposes adding every noun in the Spec File — 'page', 'button', 'filter', 'list', roughly sixty entries — arguing that a complete glossary can only help. CAS's inclusion bar (ambiguity, domain weight, or recurrence) keeps most of those out. What makes a deliberately small Dictionary load-bearing rather than stingy?
choices: Sixty entries make the Context block long, and long markdown documents are painful to edit and review; the framework keeps Dictionaries small so that definition edits stay reviewable as clean per-term diffs

Everyday UI words belong in a separate UI Context with its own Dictionary; the mistake is not listing them but putting them in a business Context, which breaks the one-vocabulary-per-Context invariant

Highlighting is a signal, and the inclusion bar keeps it honest. Every defined term must be backticked at every dictionary-sense use, so each entry taxes all future Stories and AC — and a Dictionary full of everyday words makes backticks so common they stop meaning 'this word carries a checked, shared definition'. Rule 9's grep-based propagation degrades the same way: re-review sets balloon with incidental matches. Terms earn entries via ambiguity, domain weight, or recurrence; doubtful ones stay out and the pruning pass decides
A large Dictionary makes AI-assisted drafting unreliable: generation quality drops as the terminology context grows, so the framework keeps Dictionaries small enough to fit inside a drafting prompt
questions.explanation: The Dictionary is not documentation for completeness' sake — it is an index of exactly the words where misunderstanding is plausible and costly. Its value comes from precision: when a reader hits a backticked term, that markup must reliably mean 'stop — this has a checked definition'. Sixty everyday nouns destroy the property twice over: readers learn to skim past backticks (signal dilution), and a definition change to any real term greps into a haystack of incidental matches, making Rule 9's mechanical propagation noisy exactly where it must be trusted. That is why the framework calls the inclusion bar its immune system and pairs it with recurring pruning — zero citations removes an entry, one citation gets judged, favouring lean. The distractors reach for adjacent but non-load-bearing concerns: per-term sections do give clean diffs, but that argues for the format, not the size; a UI Context would merely relocate the bloat — the words still fail the earn-your-entry test wherever they live; and prompt-size ergonomics is no framework concern — the economics being protected are those of the human reading signal.

questions.question: A product owner starts delivering 'complete' story cards: the Connextra narrative plus a full set of Given/When/Then scenarios, so the team 'can start coding without a meeting'. Reviewers keep flagging them. Given the 3Cs — Card, Conversation, Confirmation — what is the actual defect?
choices: Gherkin on a ticket is dead text: scenarios belong in version-controlled .feature files where they execute in CI, so the defect is putting the Confirmation in the wrong medium, not writing it early
Pre-written scenarios reveal the stories are too large: a card that needs many Given/When/Then blocks fails INVEST-Small, and the fix is splitting until each story needs only one or two scenarios

The scenarios create hidden coupling: each Given clause presupposes state delivered by other stories, which breaks INVEST-Independent; scenarios should only be authored for stories with no cross-story references

The card is a promise for a conversation, not a container for the requirement. Detail is meant to emerge in the Conversation, and the Confirmation — the acceptance tests — is written after it, from shared understanding. A card that arrives pre-confirmed skips the practice stories exist for: negotiability is gone because the behaviour is frozen before anyone discussed it, and the team codes to one person's untested assumptions — with a meeting-shaped hole where mutual discovery should have happened
questions.explanation: Stories are deliberately incomplete artifacts — that is their function, not a limitation. The 3Cs place the requirement's substance in the Conversation and make the Confirmation its output: acceptance criteria record what the team agreed, not what one author anticipated. Writing them upfront inverts the practice — it converts the story into a mini-spec, silently deletes the negotiation step (INVEST-Negotiable), and defers misunderstandings to code review or UAT, exactly the expensive-late-disagreement failure the practice exists to prevent. It also mixes two artifacts on one card (the 'merge' smell): narrative and AC have different authors, lifecycles, and formats. The fix is process, not formatting: keep the card light, run the conversation (Three Amigos, Example Mapping), then formulate the agreed examples as AC. The distractors mistake symptoms for the disease: where scenarios are stored says nothing about when and from whose understanding they are authored; scenario count can flag an oversized story, but these cards would be defective at any size; and Given-clause coupling is a test-design concern, not the reason a pre-confirmed card subverts the story workflow.

questions.question: A small team stores terraform.tfstate in the git repo next to the .tf files — 'state is versioned with the code that produced it, and everyone gets it on pull'. It works until two engineers apply within the same hour and the infrastructure diverges. What is wrong with git as a state store, and what is the sanctioned setup?
choices: State is a live runtime record, not source code: plan and apply need the latest state at execution time and exclusive access while writing it. Git provides neither — freshness is whenever someone last pulled, and there is no locking, so two concurrent applies each update their own copy and one write clobbers the other. State can also carry secrets in plaintext, which a repo multiplies across every clone. A remote backend (e.g. S3) is the sanctioned fix: one shared source of truth, locking during apply, access-controlled storage. Version the config; treat state like a database

The failure is merge conflicts on the JSON: state files are machine-generated and unmergeable, so the fix is marking terraform.tfstate as binary in .gitattributes and resolving conflicts by always taking the newest committed version

State records provider versions and workspace-local paths, so a state file produced on one machine fails on another; committing it can only work if the whole team pins identical Terraform and provider versions via required_providers

Git history is the problem: state contains resource IDs that the cloud provider rotates over time, so an old committed state misreads reality; a pre-apply hook running terraform refresh before every plan keeps the committed state usable
questions.explanation: The mental model that fails here is 'state is an artifact of the code, so it belongs with the code'. State is the opposite: it is Terraform's runtime database — the mapping between configuration and real resource IDs — read and rewritten on every apply. A database needs freshness and concurrency control; git offers point-in-time snapshots and no locks. The observed divergence is the textbook symptom: both engineers applied against yesterday's state, each produced a different 'truth', and the last push won. The secrets problem compounds it — state can embed passwords and generated keys in plaintext, and git distributes and preserves them in history forever. Remote backends exist precisely to give state database semantics: shared, locked, access-controlled. Note the division of labour: the .tf files absolutely belong in git — reviewable, versioned infrastructure is the IaC promise — it is only the state file that doesn't. The distractors keep git and patch around it: a conflict-resolution convention adds no locking and 'take the newest' institutionalises silently losing the other apply; state is not machine-specific (that concern belongs to the .terraform plugin directory, which is why it — not state — is merely gitignored); and refresh reconciles drift against reality but cannot serialise two concurrent applies.

questions.question: To train a 95th-percentile model, an engineer passes LightGBM a custom objective returning pinball's derivatives — grad = −α when under-predicting, 1−α otherwise, hess = 1 — reasoning this is exactly what objective='quantile' computes internally. The custom model trains, but its predictions are visibly mis-calibrated compared to the built-in objective's. What does the built-in do that the custom objective cannot?
choices: The built-in uses the exact second derivative α(1−α) rather than the placeholder 1, giving the Newton steps proper curvature; supplying that hessian from the custom objective reproduces the built-in behaviour

Those derivatives carry direction but no distance: the gradient is piecewise-constant and the hessian is a placeholder for a loss whose true curvature is zero, so the Newton leaf value −ΣG/(ΣH+λ) is a fixed-size nudge that cannot say how far a leaf must move to sit at the 95th percentile. LightGBM special-cases its built-in objective: after the tree structure is grown from the gradient signs, it renews every leaf output, overwriting it with the α-percentile of the residuals that landed in that leaf. A custom objective gets no renewal — its gradients pick the splits, but nothing calibrates the leaf values

The built-in also switches the internal evaluation metric to pinball loss at the same α, which steers early stopping toward quantile-accurate rounds; the custom run kept the default L2 metric, so early stopping selected mean-calibrated iterations

objective='quantile' reweights training rows by α on one side of the current prediction and 1−α on the other — a dynamic resampling a static gradient cannot express; passing sample weights that mirror the α asymmetry closes the gap
questions.explanation: The gradient-boosting machinery assumes a loss whose derivatives encode both direction and local scale. Pinball loss breaks that contract: it is piecewise-linear, so its gradient only says 'above or below' (weighted α versus 1−α), and its honest second derivative is zero — the h = 1 is a solver-appeasing placeholder. Newton leaf values computed from such inputs know which way to move but not how far, and no number of boosting rounds reliably lands them on the target quantile. LightGBM's fix is architectural, marked IsRenewTreeOutput() in the source: split-finding and leaf valuation are decoupled. Gradient signs shape the tree; then each leaf's value is replaced by the weighted α-percentile of its own residuals — an order statistic computed directly, not descended to. That renewal step is a privilege of the built-in objective: the custom-objective API only accepts g and h, so it can reproduce the tree shapes but never the calibrated leaf values. The distractors offer plausible levers that don't exist here: α(1−α) is the Bernoulli variance from logistic loss, not a pinball hessian — the true one is 0; the eval metric influences early stopping, not per-leaf calibration; and no row-reweighting step exists inside the quantile objective.

questions.question: In review you find: const [total, setTotal] = useState(0) plus useEffect(() => { setTotal(price * quantity) }, [price, quantity]). The author defends it: 'total updates whenever its inputs change — that is what effects are for.' What is the objection, and the idiomatic rewrite?
choices: The only real defect is the first paint showing 0 before the effect fires; initializing the state lazily with useState(() => price * quantity) removes the flash and makes the effect-sync pattern sound

The dependency array is incomplete: setTotal comes from component scope and belongs in it; omitting it risks calling a stale setter after re-renders, which is exactly what exhaustive-deps guards against

total is derivable from values the component already has, so storing it creates a second source of truth that is wrong by construction for one render: effects run after commit, so every input change paints a stale total first, then re-renders. The pairing also invites drift — any future code path that updates one without the other desynchronizes the UI. Effects exist to synchronize with external systems, and nothing external is involved. Delete the state and the effect and compute during render: const total = price * quantity. The review heuristic: for each useEffect, ask which external system it synchronizes with — if the answer is 'none', it should not be an effect

Because React batches state updates, setTotal(price * quantity) inside an effect can read a stale snapshot of price; the updater form setTotal(() => price * quantity) defers the read to apply time and fixes the synchronization
questions.explanation: The render model makes this pattern structurally worse than it looks: setting state from an effect forces a second render pass on every input change — render with the stale total, commit, run the effect, set state, render again — which is both wasted work and a visible one-frame lie. The deeper objection is architectural: redundant state. React's own design method ('find the minimal but complete representation of state') classifies anything computable from existing props and state as derived data — compute it during render and it is correct on the same pass, always, with no synchronization machinery to maintain or forget. State-plus-effect is reserved for values React cannot derive: subscriptions, fetches, browser APIs. The distractors all accept the redundant state and tune its plumbing: lazy initialization fixes only the first frame while keeping the double render and the drift risk; useState setters are guaranteed stable and never belong in dependency arrays; and the updater form addresses updates computed from previous state, not closure staleness over props — the effect's closure already sees the values of the render that scheduled it.

questions.question: An attachments endpoint serializes rows that point at either an Order or an Invoice. Product wants invoice rows to carry an invoice_number field and order rows to not have the key at all — not even as null. A developer tries declaring the field conditionally in the serializer's __init__ based on the instance, and it misbehaves on list endpoints. What is the sanctioned DRF pattern?
choices: Declare two serializers — OrderAttachmentSerializer and InvoiceAttachmentSerializer — and override the viewset's get_serializer_class() to pick by the object's entity_type; DRF instantiates the right one per object, so mixed lists come out correctly typed
Return None from a SerializerMethodField and configure the JSON renderer to omit null values globally; the wire drops the key with no per-serializer code at all
Split the API into /orders/{id}/attachments/ and /invoices/{id}/attachments/ with a dedicated serializer each; a single polymorphic list endpoint fighting its serializer is the actual design smell

Serializer fields are class-level declarations evaluated once at import — one serializer instance serves every row of a list, so per-row field presence cannot be expressed in declarations or __init__. The shaping hook is to_representation(instance): declare invoice_number as a SerializerMethodField for all rows (returning None where inapplicable), then override to_representation, call super() to build the full dict, and pop the keys that don't apply to that row — the add-then-strip idiom. Declarations stay static; per-row variation lives in the one hook DRF calls per instance
questions.explanation: The failure teaches DRF's layering: a serializer class describes a wire schema — static, fixed at import time — while to_representation is the per-instance escape hatch, the last stop before JSON encoding, called once per row even under many=True. Trying to make the declarations dynamic fights the first layer with information that belongs to the second: on a list endpoint __init__ runs once, sees no single row, and whatever field set it settles on applies uniformly to every element. Add-then-strip respects the layers — the method field computes what it can (None where not applicable), and the per-row hook trims each dict so every entity_type gets a typed shape with no null noise; consumers never learn to ignore junk keys. The distractors relocate the problem without solving it: get_serializer_class chooses one class per request, not per row — a mixed list still renders through a single serializer; a null-dropping renderer is a global blunt instrument DRF doesn't ship as a flag, and it would also strip legitimate nulls on every other endpoint; and splitting the endpoints is a defensible API-design debate, but it abandons the stated requirement — one attachments list — rather than implementing it.

questions.question: A backend stores user uploads in S3. For the local Docker stack a teammate proposes skipping MinIO: 'just add an if settings.LOCAL: save-to-a-local-folder branch — one less container, and the code is trivial.' The team runs MinIO instead. What is the architectural argument that justifies the extra container?
choices: The branch is acceptable only behind a storage interface: define a StorageBackend protocol with S3 and filesystem implementations, inject one per environment, and both paths become swappable and unit-testable — the real mistake was the naked if, not the second backend

The filesystem branch is code production never executes and local runs never skip — so the S3 path, the one that matters, is exercised only after deploy, and the fallback drifts silently as the two implementations diverge. MinIO removes the branch instead of dressing it up: it serves the real S3 API, so the identical boto3 code path runs everywhere and only configuration changes — endpoint URL and credentials. Vary environments by config, not by code: dev/prod parity applied to storage

A local folder cannot reproduce object-store semantics at all — keys containing slashes, per-object metadata, and content types have no filesystem equivalent — so the branch would not even work for realistic uploads; MinIO is the only way to run the feature locally

Branching on a debug-style LOCAL flag is the flaw — such flags change many behaviours at once; keying the branch on a dedicated STORAGE_BACKEND variable isolates the decision and makes the filesystem path safe to keep
questions.explanation: The question is what the local environment is for: if it exists to validate what ships, every branch that substitutes a different implementation locally subtracts from that validation. The if LOCAL branch creates a path asymmetry — the code you exercise daily is not the code you run in production, and the code you run in production is first exercised after deploy. Bugs living in the S3 interaction itself (addressing style, credential wiring, error shapes, bucket assumptions) can only surface in the cloud. MinIO's value is precisely that it is not a mock: it implements the S3 API as a real server, so swapping AWS for MinIO is a change of address, not of code — the local stack drives the same boto3 client through the same calls and failure modes. The distractors settle for smaller wins: the interface abstraction is good design but keeps two implementations, and the S3 one still goes unexercised locally — parity is about which code runs, not how cleanly it is factored; the capability-gap claim overreaches — a filesystem can emulate keys and metadata well enough to pass tests, which is exactly how the drift stays silent; and renaming the flag improves configuration hygiene while leaving the untested-branch problem intact.

questions.question: A Django service wraps an upload flow in transaction.atomic: it calls storage.save() to push the file to S3, creates the Attachment row, and then a later validation step raises. The row is rolled back — but the object is still in the bucket, orphaned. A teammate proposes 'moving storage.save() deeper inside the atomic block so it joins the transaction.' Why can't that work, and what is the honest pattern?
choices: The mistake is calling storage.save() manually: assigning the upload to the model's FileField and letting model.save() persist both makes Django coordinate the file write with the row write inside the transaction

Nested atomic blocks create savepoints, and a savepoint taken before storage.save() lets the rollback restore both the row and the file; the code just needs the storage call wrapped in its own inner atomic block

transaction.atomic governs exactly one system: the database connection. S3 does not participate in that transaction — wherever the call sits inside the block, a rollback cannot un-PUT an object, because the guarantee never extended past the DB. Side effects on external systems need explicit compensation: keep the blob write and the row write adjacent, and on failure delete the stored object in an except branch — write, then compensate — or defer the external write until after commit. The design habit: know which operations are inside the transactional boundary and which only look like they are
Enabling bucket versioning dissolves the problem: the orphaned PUT becomes a non-current version that lifecycle rules expire, giving storage the same all-or-nothing semantics the database provides
questions.explanation: A transaction is a contract with one resource manager — here, the database. Everything inside atomic is provisional until commit because the database itself holds the machinery (undo logs, savepoints) to revoke it. An HTTP PUT to an object store carries no such machinery: the moment it returns, the object exists, and your connection's eventual COMMIT or ROLLBACK is invisible to S3. Placement inside the block is therefore cosmetic — this is the distributed-transaction boundary, and pretending a code block spans it is how orphaned blobs (or worse, committed rows pointing at never-written files) are born. Honest patterns acknowledge the two systems: compensate on failure — a try/except that deletes the stored object, a saga in miniature — or reorder so the external write happens only once the DB outcome is known (transaction.on_commit is the Django hook for the latter). Tests share the blind spot: TestCase rolls back DB writes, but storage writes persist unless explicitly cleaned. The distractors dress the gap in Django idioms: FileField assignment changes who calls storage, not its transactionality; savepoints are database-internal markers no external system honours; and versioning changes what an orphan looks like — an expiring non-current version is still a write the rollback never undid.
